mainTopic: Women held by non-Jews: money versus capital cases, and wives of כהנים in a captured city, including when a hiding place saves them.
overview: Our משנה says a woman held by non-Jews over money stays permitted to her husband, but one held over a capital case is forbidden. The גמרא tests רב's limit, that the money rule applies only when the Jews' hand is strong, against the Ashkelon testimony in עדויות, told in three versions. In the end, רב שמואל בר רב יצחק explains that the משנה speaks of a time when the Jews are strong, and Ashkelon of a time when the non-Jews are fully in control. For the capital case, רב and לוי give examples, and חזקיה and רבי יוחנן argue whether the death sentence must already be final. A new משנה rules that wives of כהנים in a city captured by a siege army are forbidden unless witnesses, even a slave or maidservant, testify for them. The גמרא raises a contradiction from wine barrels in wartime and answers it in two ways: soldiers find time for desire but not for idol wine, or the city's own army is different from a foreign army. Then a single hiding place is said to save all the wives. רבי ירמיה asks what happens if it fits only one woman, and the comparison to the two-paths case is rejected, since here maybe no woman was harmed at all. The amud ends as רב אשי asks about a woman who says she did not hide and was not defiled; the discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Taken as security is different from imprisoned
steps.stepSummary: The end of רבא's challenge: the Ashkelon testimony was about a woman taken as security, which suggests an imprisoned woman would not need witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: If she was taken as security, yes, she needs witnesses. If she was imprisoned, no.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a challenge to רב. The Ashkelon case suggests the deciding factor is how she was taken, not whose hand is strong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב said a woman held over money is forbidden only when the non-Jews' hand is strong. The challenge reads the Ashkelon case as drawing a different line: הורהנה (her husband handed her over as security) is dangerous, but נחבשה (simply imprisoned) is not. If so, the real factor is the type of capture, not political strength.

keyTerms.meaning: She was taken as security, held as collateral for a debt
She was imprisoned, held by the authorities

phrases.english: If she was taken as security, yes [she needs witnesses],
if she was imprisoned, no.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Concludes the challenge to רב that began before this section.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's rule that a woman held over money is forbidden when the non-Jews' hand is strong.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Ashkelon case suggests the deciding factor is the manner of capture (security versus imprisonment), not who holds power.

steps.title: Imprisonment is the same; the story just happened that way
steps.stepSummary: The same law applies to an imprisoned woman. The testimony mentions security only because that is what actually happened.
steps.simpleTranslation: The same is true even if she was imprisoned. The incident that happened simply happened that way.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The detail 'taken as security' is not a legal condition; it just describes the real event.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge built a rule out of the word הורהנה. The answer says the wording reports the facts and is not meant to exclude anything. So רב's rule stands: when the non-Jews' hand is strong, even an imprisoned woman needs witnesses.

keyTerms.meaning: The incident that happened, happened that way (a real story, not a chosen example)

steps.whatToRemember: A detail in a real-life story may just be what happened. It is not always a legal condition.

phrases.english: The same law applies even if she was imprisoned.
And the incident that happened, happened that way.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 1.
steps.terutzResolutionType: The wording reflects the actual event, not a legal distinction.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: That 'taken as security' was chosen to exclude imprisonment.
steps.terutzMaskana: Imprisonment is treated the same, so רב's rule holds.

steps.title: Second version: רבא supports רב from the Ashkelon case
steps.stepSummary: In another version, רבא brings the Ashkelon testimony as support for רב rather than as a challenge.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say: רבא said, we too learned this. רבי יוסי הכהן and רבי זכריה בן הקצב testified about a Jewish woman taken as security in Ashkelon. Her family kept away from her, and her witnesses testified that she was not secluded and not defiled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a different version of רבא's words, in which he uses the same source to support רב. This step sets out the case; the proof comes in step 5.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version רבא is on רב's side. The facts matter: the woman was held over money, yet her family worried about her. Witnesses were needed to show she stayed pure.

keyTerms.meaning: We too have learned it (support from a משנה)
Testified (a teaching passed down by testimony)
Was secluded alone with a man

phrases.english: Some say: רבא said:
We too have learned this:
phrases.notes: He means we have support for רב's rule from a משנה in עדויות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei the Kohen testified
and Rabbi Zecharya ben HaKatzav,
about a Jewish woman who was taken as security in Ashkelon,
and her family members kept away from her,
and her witnesses testify about her
that she was not secluded and was not defiled.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִיכָּא דְּאָמְרִי, אָמַר רָבָא: אַף אֲנַן נָמֵי תְּנֵינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Restarts the discussion in a second version, now as support for רב.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that a woman held over money is forbidden when the non-Jews' hand is strong.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה in עדויות about the woman held as security in Ashkelon.

steps.title: The Sages' argument to the family
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים tell the family to believe the witnesses fully or not at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages said: if you believe she was taken as security, believe that she was not secluded and not defiled. If you don't believe that, don't believe she was taken as security either.
steps.whatsHappening: This continues the quote from the משנה: the חכמים' ruling in the Ashkelon case. It finishes setting up the proof that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone knows about the capture only from the same witnesses. So you cannot accept the bad part of their story and reject the good part. The woman is permitted because of the witnesses' testimony.

phrases.english: And the Sages said:
If you believe [the witnesses] that she was taken as security,
then believe that she was not secluded and was not defiled.
And if you do not believe
that she was not secluded and was not defiled,
do not believe that she was taken as security.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמְרוּ חֲכָמִים: אִם אַתֶּם מַאֲמִינִים שֶׁהוּרְהֲנָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the quote of the source begun in step 3.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Witnesses who report the capture are also believed when they say she stayed pure, so she is permitted.

steps.title: Even over money, she needed witnesses
steps.stepSummary: רבא's proof: Ashkelon was a money case, yet she was permitted only because of witnesses. So when the non-Jews' hand is strong, even imprisonment over money is a concern.
steps.simpleTranslation: But Ashkelon was over money, and the reason she is permitted is that witnesses testify for her. Without witnesses, no. Doesn't this show there is no difference between being taken as security and being imprisoned?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא draws his proof for רב from the Ashkelon case. Even in a money case, she needed witnesses.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Our משנה says a money case leaves her permitted without witnesses. Ashkelon, where the non-Jews were strong, needed witnesses. רבא reads this as covering any capture over money, imprisonment included, which matches רב's limit.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of money (a financial matter, not a capital crime)
Is it not that... (introduces the proposed proof)

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא אַשְׁקְלוֹן, דְּעַל יְדֵי מָמוֹן הֲוָה,
phrases.english: But Ashkelon was a case over money,
and the reason [she is permitted] is that witnesses testify for her;

phrases.aramaic: הָא אֵין עֵדִים מְעִידִין אוֹתָהּ — לָא.
phrases.english: if no witnesses testify for her, no [she would not be permitted].
Is it not that

phrases.aramaic: לָא שְׁנָא הוּרְהֲנָה, וְלָא שְׁנָא נֶחְבְּשָׁה!
phrases.english: it makes no difference whether she was taken as security or imprisoned!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָא אַשְׁקְלוֹן, דְּעַל יְדֵי מָמוֹן הֲוָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the proof from the source quoted in steps 3 and 4.
steps.raayaObject: רב's rule that when the non-Jews' hand is strong, a woman held over money needs witnesses.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The inference from the Ashkelon case: without witnesses she would be forbidden, even in a money case.

steps.title: Taken as security is a special case
steps.stepSummary: The proof is rejected: being taken as security is different, so the case says nothing about imprisonment.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Being taken as security is different.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away רבא's proof. Ashkelon may be a special case because she was handed over as security.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When a husband hands his wife over as security, her captors feel freer to treat her as their own, so witnesses are needed. That worry may not apply to a woman simply imprisoned. So Ashkelon does not prove רב's broader rule.
steps.confusionAlert: This is the same distinction the challenge raised in step 1. There it was answered; here it is used to reject a proof. The two steps belong to different versions, so they do not contradict each other.

phrases.english: No. Being taken as security is different.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof in step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof from Ashkelon, not רב's rule itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed security and imprisonment are the same, but security may carry a special risk.

steps.title: Third version: the Ashkelon case contradicts our משנה
steps.stepSummary: Some use the Ashkelon case to contradict our משנה directly. Our משנה permits a woman held over money, but in Ashkelon she needed witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some raise it as a contradiction. We learned: if it was over money, she is permitted to her husband. But they raise a contradiction from 'רבי יוסי testified' and so on. Ashkelon was over money, yet it teaches that she is permitted because witnesses testify for her. Without witnesses, no!
steps.whatsHappening: A third version sets the two sources against each other. One says a money case is fine without witnesses; the other required witnesses. The next step answers this.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the Ashkelon case is not a challenge to רב or a proof for him. It is a direct clash with our משנה. Step 8 resolves it with the distinction about whose hand is strong.

keyTerms.meaning: Raises it as a contradiction between two sources
And they raised a contradiction from another source

phrases.english: Some raise it as a contradiction:

phrases.aramaic: תְּנַן: עַל יְדֵי מָמוֹן מוּתֶּרֶת לְבַעְלָהּ,
phrases.english: We learned: [if held] over money, she is permitted to her husband.
And they raised a contradiction: 'Rabbi Yosei testified,' etc.
phrases.notes: 'Etc.' points back to the whole Ashkelon testimony quoted in steps 3 and 4.

phrases.english: But Ashkelon was over money,
and it teaches that the reason [she is permitted] is that witnesses testify for her;

phrases.aramaic: הָא אֵין עֵדִים מְעִידִין אוֹתָהּ לָא!
phrases.english: if no witnesses testify for her, no!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents a third version, using the same source to contradict our משנה directly.
steps.kashyaTarget: Our משנה: a woman held over money stays permitted to her husband.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The Ashkelon case was also over money, yet she needed witnesses, which clashes with the משנה.

steps.title: It depends on who holds power
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק settles the contradiction between our משנה and the Ashkelon case. Our משנה speaks of a time when Jews are strong. Ashkelon was a time when the non-Jews were in control.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he answers: רב שמואל בר רב יצחק said: It is not difficult. Here, our משנה speaks of a time when Israel's hand is strong over the nations. There, in Ashkelon, it was a time when the nations' hand was strong over themselves.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction from Step 7. Both rulings are correct, but they fit different times.
steps.deeperAnalysis: When Jews have power, non-Jews holding a woman over money will not risk harming her, so she stays permitted. When the non-Jews are fully in control, they fear nothing, so even a woman held over money needs witnesses. The rule for money cases is not cancelled. Its outcome changes with the political situation.

keyTerms.meaning: It is not difficult; both sources can be true
A strong hand; having power and control
The nations of the world; non-Jews

steps.whatToRemember: In a money case, she is permitted only when the Jews have power. When non-Jews are fully in control, even a money case needs witnesses.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows the משנה's rule depends on the real-world risk, not just on the type of case.

phrases.aramaic: וּמְשַׁנֵּי, אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק,
phrases.english: And he answers: Rav Shmuel bar Rav Yitzchak said:
It is not difficult.
Here, it is when the hand of Israel is strong
phrases.notes: 'Here' is our משנה, which permits a woman held over money. 'There' in the next line is the Ashkelon case, where she needed witnesses.

phrases.english: over the nations of the world;
there, it is when the hand of the nations of the world
is strong over themselves.
phrases.notes: He means the non-Jews answer to no one and are fully in charge.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְשַׁנֵּי, אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר רַב יִצְחָק, לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in Step 7
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Our משנה and the Ashkelon case seem to rule differently on a woman held over money.
steps.terutzMaskana: Our משנה applies when Jews are strong. Ashkelon applies when non-Jews are fully in control.

steps.title: Which capital cases does the משנה mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's rule that a woman held over a capital case is forbidden. רב says this includes wives of thieves. לוי says it means a case like the wife of בן דונאי.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: 'Through a capital case she is forbidden, etc.' רב said: For example, the wives of thieves. And לוי said: For example, the wife of בן דונאי.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the second half of the משנה, about a woman held over a capital case. Two אמוראים give examples of what this means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a capital case, the husband is facing death, so the captors no longer hold back from the wife. רב includes thieves, since they too were executed and their wives left unprotected. לוי gives the example of בן דונאי, a much more serious criminal, and suggests the concern applies only to cases like that.

keyTerms.meaning: Capital cases, where a life is at stake
A well-known murderer of that time

phrases.english: "Through a capital case she is forbidden, etc."
Rav said: For example, the wives of thieves.
And Levi said:
For example, the wife of ben Donai.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the money-case discussion to the משנה's capital-case clause
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב: a capital case includes thieves' wives. לוי: it means a case like בן דונאי's wife.

steps.title: Must the death sentence already be final?
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה says the woman is forbidden only once the husband's death sentence has been decided. רבי יוחנן says she is forbidden even before it is decided.
steps.simpleTranslation: חזקיה said: This is only when their sentence was already decided for death. And רבי יוחנן said: Even if their sentence was not yet decided for death.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים argue about when the capital-case concern begins.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה holds that captors drop all restraint only once the husband is sure to be killed. רבי יוחנן holds that a capital charge alone is enough to put the wife at risk, even before a final verdict.
steps.whatToRemember: Capital case: חזקיה requires a final death sentence. רבי יוחנן says even a pending capital charge is enough.

phrases.english: Chizkiya said:
And this is only where their sentence was decided for death.
phrases.notes: 'Their' means the husbands who were arrested.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said:
Even though it was not decided,
their sentence for death.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר חִזְקִיָּה: וְהוּא שֶׁנִּגְמַר דִּינָן לַהֲרִיגָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second point to the capital-case clause: when the concern begins
steps.mimraCoreRuling: חזקיה: only after a final death sentence. רבי יוחנן: even before a final sentence.

steps.title: Wives of כהנים in a conquered city
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה: when a siege army conquers a city, all wives of כהנים inside become forbidden. Witnesses, even a slave or maidservant, are believed to clear them. A woman cannot clear herself.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: A city that a siege army conquered: all wives of כהנים found inside it are disqualified. And if they have witnesses, even a slave, even a maidservant, these are believed. But a person is not believed about herself.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It rules on wives of כהנים after an army captures their city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The concern is that soldiers may have violated the women, which would forbid them to a כהן. Because this is only a doubt, the משנה is lenient about who may testify, even a slave or maidservant. The woman's own word is still not enough.

keyTerms.meaning: An army laying siege around a city
A slave, a maidservant (normally not valid witnesses)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a case of a single captive woman. The whole city fell, so every כהן's wife there is under suspicion unless someone testifies for her.

phrases.english: MISHNA: A city that a siege army conquered:
all wives of priests found inside it are disqualified.
phrases.notes: Disqualified means forbidden to their כהן husbands, out of concern they were violated.

phrases.english: And if they have witnesses,
even a slave, even a maidservant,
these are believed.

phrases.aramaic: וְאֵין נֶאֱמָן אָדָם עַל יְדֵי עַצְמוֹ.
phrases.english: But a person is not believed about himself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה on a related topic: women at risk from non-Jewish soldiers
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In a conquered city, wives of כהנים are forbidden unless witnesses, even a slave or maidservant, testify. A woman cannot testify for herself.

steps.title: Wartime wine barrels seem to contradict the משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא contradicts the new משנה with a rule about wine. When soldiers enter a city in wartime, even open barrels stay permitted because they have no time to pour wine for idols. So why worry that they had time for the women?
steps.simpleTranslation: And contradict it from this: A troop that came into a city: in peacetime, open barrels are forbidden and sealed ones are permitted. In wartime, both kinds are permitted, because there is no free time to pour wine for idols.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises a contradiction against the new משנה. רב מרי answers it in the next step, and חזקיה gives another answer after that.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The wine rule assumes soldiers at war are too busy to stop for anything. If so, they should also be too busy to harm the women, and the wives of כהנים should be permitted. Yet our משנה forbids them, so the two rulings seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: To pour wine as an offering to idols

phrases.english: GEMARA: And contradict it from this:
phrases.notes: The source quoted here is a משנה in עבודה זרה.

phrases.english: A troop that came into a city:
in a time of peace,
open barrels are forbidden,
sealed ones are permitted.
In a time of war,
both these and those are permitted,
because there is no free time to pour libations.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the משנה just quoted in Step 11
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that wives of כהנים in a conquered city are forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The wine rule says soldiers at war have no time to stop. So they should not have had time to harm the women either, and the women should be permitted.

steps.title: Time for sin, but no time for idol wine
steps.stepSummary: רב מרי answers the contradiction. Soldiers will find time to violate women, but they will not stop to pour wine for idols.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב מרי said: For relations there is time; for pouring wine to idols there is no time.
steps.whatsHappening: רב מרי gives the first answer to the question from step 12. He says the two cases are simply different.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question assumed that a rushed soldier has no time for anything. רב מרי says that is not so: a soldier will make time to satisfy his desire, but he will not bother stopping for a religious act like pouring wine. So the wine stays permitted while the women are a real concern.

keyTerms.meaning: to have relations with a woman
to pour wine as an offering to an idol
free time, a chance to do something

phrases.english: Rav Mari said:
To have relations, there is time;
to pour wine for idols, there is no time.

steps.triggerLanguage: לִבְעוֹל יֵשׁ פְּנַאי, לְנַסֵּךְ אֵין פְּנַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the contradiction raised in step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between the two acts: one happens even in a rush, the other does not.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If the soldiers have no time to pour wine, they have no time to violate women either.
steps.terutzMaskana: Desire makes soldiers find time. A religious act like pouring wine is not worth stopping for.

steps.title: Same government versus a foreign government
steps.stepSummary: חזקיה, quoted by רבי יצחק בר אלעזר, gives a different answer. The wine case is a siege by the city's own government, and our משנה is a siege by a foreign government.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יצחק בר אלעזר said in the name of חזקיה: Here it is a siege by that same kingdom; there it is a siege by a different kingdom.
steps.whatsHappening: This is a second, separate answer to the contradiction. It divides the two rules by who is attacking the city.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An army of the city's own king wants to keep the city whole, so the soldiers are held back from ruining wine or harming women. That is the wine case, where everything stays permitted. A foreign army has no such restraint, and that is our משנה, where the women become forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: a siege army surrounding a city

steps.confusionAlert: The first 'כאן' (same kingdom) is the wine case, where things stay permitted. The second 'כאן' (a different kingdom) is our משנה, where the women become forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר אֶלְעָזָר מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּחִזְקִיָּה אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yitzchak bar Elazar said in the name of Chizkiyah:
Here it is a siege army of that same kingdom,
phrases.notes: This is the wine case. The city's own army does not want to wreck its own city.

phrases.english: here it is a siege army of a different kingdom.

steps.triggerLanguage: כָּאן בְּכַרְכּוֹם שֶׁל אוֹתָהּ מַלְכוּת, כָּאן בְּכַרְכּוֹם שֶׁל מַלְכוּת אַחֶרֶת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different answer to the same question from step 12, instead of רב מרי's answer.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases: the two rules speak about different kinds of armies.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both rules are about the same kind of siege, so they contradict each other.
steps.terutzMaskana: The wine rule is about the city's own army, which holds back. Our משנה is about a foreign army, which does not.

steps.title: One soldier could still slip away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges חזקיה's answer. Even in the city's own army, surely one soldier would sneak off and do harm.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even with that same kingdom, it is impossible that one of them did not run off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the 'same kingdom' answer. Orders from above cannot stop every single soldier.
steps.deeperAnalysis: חזקיה's answer depended on the army being under control. The גמרא says that in a big army at least one soldier will break away. If so, the wine should also be at risk in the 'same kingdom' case.

phrases.english: With that same kingdom too,

phrases.aramaic: אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלָא עָרַק חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ.
phrases.english: it is impossible that one of them did not run off.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלָא עָרַק חַד מִינַּיְיהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 14.
steps.kashyaTarget: חזקיה's claim that an army of the same kingdom does no damage.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: No army is fully disciplined. One soldier slipping away is enough to create the worry.

steps.title: The guards can see each other
steps.stepSummary: שמואל, quoted by רב יהודה, answers that the case is where the guard posts can see one another, so no soldier can slip away.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said in the name of שמואל: It is a case where the guard posts can see one another.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends the 'same kingdom' answer. It describes a tightly watched army where nobody can sneak off.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the guards are placed close enough to see each other, any soldier who tries to leave will be spotted. This narrows the case so the challenge of step 15 no longer applies.

phrases.english: Rav Yehudah said in the name of Shmuel:
When the guard posts see one another.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 15.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case to a tightly guarded siege.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Some soldier will surely escape and cause harm.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is one where the guards watch each other, so nobody can slip away.

steps.title: The guards might doze off
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes back again. Surely the guards will nap a little at some point.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is impossible that they would not doze a little!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל's answer. Guards are human and will sleep a bit.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even guards who can see each other cannot stay awake the whole time. A short nap is enough for a soldier to sneak into the city.

phrases.english: It is impossible that they would not doze a little!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's answer that the guards seeing each other stops anyone from slipping away.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Guards will nap at some point. During that gap a soldier can get in.

steps.title: A city sealed with chains, dogs, branches and geese
steps.stepSummary: רבי לוי answers that the city is surrounded with chains, dogs, branches and geese. Nobody can get in without being stopped or heard.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי לוי said: For example, where they surround the city with chains, dogs, branches and geese.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי לוי gives the final defense of the 'same kingdom' answer. The city is sealed so well that even a dozing guard does not matter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The chains and branches block the way. The dogs and geese make noise if anyone comes near. So even if a guard naps, no soldier can sneak in quietly.

phrases.english: Rabbi Levi said:
For example, where they surround the city with
chains, and dogs, and branches, and geese.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּגוֹן דִּמְהַדַּר לַהּ לְמָתָא שׁוּשִׁילְתָּא וְכַלְבָּא וּגְווֹזָא וַאֲווֹזָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 17 and ends this back-and-forth.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case further to a fully sealed city.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A napping guard leaves a gap for a soldier to sneak in.
steps.terutzMaskana: The city is ringed with blocks and noisy animals, so no one can enter unnoticed.

steps.title: Two sages, two ways of reading the same answer
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא בר זבדא reports that רבי יהודה נשיאה and the רבנן disagree. One gave the 'same kingdom' answer and saw no problem with it. The other felt all the challenges and needed the sealed city with chains, dogs, branches and geese.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא בר זבדא said: רבי יהודה נשיאה and the רבנן disagree about this. One said: here it is the same kingdom, there a different kingdom, and nothing was difficult for him. For the other, all these were difficult, and he answers: for example, where they surround the city with chains, dogs, branches and geese.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא looks back over the whole discussion and reports that it was a real disagreement between two sages. They differ on how much the 'same kingdom' answer needs to be propped up.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first sage thought the city's own army simply does not cause harm, so the challenges about runaway soldiers and sleepy guards never bothered him. The second sage took those challenges seriously. He limited the case to a city sealed off completely.

keyTerms.meaning: a later leader of the Jewish people, grandson of רבי יהודה הנשיא

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain why the wine stays permitted but the women become forbidden. One is רב מרי's: soldiers find time for desire but not for pouring wine. The other is חזקיה's: the city's own army versus a foreign army. Some held that the 'same kingdom' answer works only if the city is fully sealed off.

phrases.english: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said:

phrases.aramaic: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה וְרַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: Rabbi Yehudah Nesiah and the Rabbis disagree about this.
One said:
Here it is a siege army of that same kingdom,
here it is a siege army of a different kingdom,
and nothing at all was difficult for him.
phrases.notes: He did not feel the challenges from steps 15 and 17 about runaway soldiers and sleepy guards.

phrases.english: And for the other one, all these were difficult,
and he answers:
For example, where they surround the city with
chains, and dogs, and branches, and geese.

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּלִיגִי בַּהּ רַבִּי יְהוּדָה נְשִׂיאָה וְרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Sums up the back-and-forth of steps 14 to 18 as a disagreement between two sages.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One sage accepts the 'same kingdom' answer as it stands. The other requires a fully sealed city for it to work.

steps.title: One hiding place saves all the women
steps.stepSummary: רבי יצחק בר אשיאן, quoted by רב אידי בר אבין, rules that if there is even one hiding place in the city, all the wives of כהנים stay permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אידי בר אבין said in the name of רבי יצחק בר אשיאן: If there is even one hiding place there, it saves all the כהנים's wives.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the משנה from step 11 and adds a new rule. A single hiding place in the city keeps every כהן's wife permitted.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said all the wives of כהנים in a captured city become forbidden. This rule limits that. If there was a place to hide, each woman might have hidden there, so we do not assume she was violated and she stays permitted to her husband.
steps.confusionAlert: 'One' hiding place means a single spot, not one per woman. The ruling does not say how many women it holds. Whether a spot with room for only one woman also helps is רבי ירמיה's open question in the next step.
steps.whyThisMatters: It sharply limits the משנה's rule. In practice, a woman in a captured city is forbidden to her כהן husband only if there was no place at all to hide.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב אִידִי בַּר אָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יִצְחָק בַּר אַשְׁיָאן:
phrases.english: Rav Idi bar Avin said in the name of Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan:
If there is a single hiding place there,
it saves all the wives of the Kohanim.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִם יֵשׁ שָׁם מַחְבּוֹאָה אַחַת מַצֶּלֶת עַל הַכֹּהֲנוֹת כּוּלָּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the wine contradiction and goes back to the משנה from step 11 to limit its rule.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the city had even one hiding place, every כהן's wife stays permitted, since each might have hidden there.

steps.title: What if the hiding place fits only one woman?
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה asks whether a hiding place that holds only one woman can still permit every wife.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה asked: if the hiding place can hold only one woman, what is the law? Do we say about each woman, 'she is the one who hid there'? Or do we not say that?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ירמיה asks a follow-up question on the rule from step 20. What happens if the hiding spot is so small that only one woman could have hidden in it?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 20, one hiding place was enough to permit all the wives. But if only one woman could fit, then at most one woman was actually safe. The question is whether we may still give each woman, one at a time, the benefit of the doubt.

keyTerms.meaning: He asked a question, an open legal question

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya asked:
If it holds only one, what is the law?
phrases.notes: 'It' is the hiding place from the last ruling, where one hiding spot kept all the wives permitted.

phrases.english: Do we say
about each and every one, 'this is the one who hid,'
or perhaps we do not say that?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limit of רבי יצחק בר אשיאן's ruling from step 20 by making the hiding place fit only one woman.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does a hiding place that fits only one woman still permit each wife, judged one at a time?

steps.title: Comparing to the case of two paths
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings up the case of two paths, one impure and one pure, with two people who each walked on one.
steps.simpleTranslation: How is this different from two paths, one impure and one pure? One person walked on one of them and then handled pure items. His friend came, walked on the other path, and also handled pure items.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that each woman could be permitted by comparing it to a known case. This step only sets up the case. The ruling comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With two paths, one person surely walked on the impure path, but we do not know which one. That is just like the small hiding place: at most one woman was safe, but we do not know which. So the two-paths case can teach us the answer.

keyTerms.meaning: And how is it different? (a challenge from a similar case)
Items that must be kept ritually pure

phrases.english: And how is this different from two paths,
one impure and one pure?
And someone walked on one of them
and then handled pure items,
and his friend came and walked on the second path
and also handled pure items,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for רבי ירמיה's question: the similar two-paths case seems to settle it strictly.
steps.kashyaTarget: The option that each woman can be permitted on her own.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the two-paths case one person is surely impure, just as here at most one woman was safe. So the same rule should apply.

steps.title: רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי argue about the two paths
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says asking separately makes the items pure and asking together makes them impure. רבי יוסי says they are impure either way.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: if each one asked on his own, the items are pure. If both asked together, they are impure. רבי יוסי says: either way they are impure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the ruling of the two-paths משנה. רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי disagree about it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהודה, each person alone has a real doubt, so he stays pure. But if they come together, we cannot call both of them pure, since one of them surely walked on the impure path. רבי יוסי treats them as impure even when they ask separately.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
If this one asked on his own
and that one asked on his own,
the items are pure.
If both asked together, the items are impure.
Rabbi Yosei says:
Either way, they are impure.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the ruling for the two-paths case introduced in step 22.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהודה: asking separately makes the items pure, asking together makes them impure. רבי יוסי: impure in both cases.

steps.title: Where exactly רבי יהודה and רבי יוסי disagree
steps.stepSummary: רבא (or רבי יוחנן) explains that everyone agrees about 'together' and 'one after the other.' They argue only when one person asks about himself and his friend.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא, and some say רבי יוחנן, said: if they come at the same time, everyone agrees they are impure. If they come one after the other, everyone agrees they are pure. They argue only when one person comes to ask about himself and about his friend. One Sage compares this to 'at the same time,' and the other compares it to 'one after the other.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא clarifies the argument from step 23 and makes it much narrower.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even רבי יוסי agrees that two people asking separately are pure. Even רבי יהודה agrees that two people asking together are impure. The only argument is about one person asking about both cases. רבי יוסי says this counts as 'together,' and רבי יהודה says it counts as 'one after the other.'
steps.confusionAlert: Don't read step 23 to mean רבי יוסי makes even two separate askers impure. רבא explains that everyone agrees separate askers are pure. The argument is only about one person who asks about both cases.

phrases.english: And Rava said, and some say it was Rabbi Yochanan:
If they come at the same time, everyone agrees they are impure.

phrases.aramaic: בְּזֶה אַחַר זֶה — דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל: טְהוֹרִים.
phrases.english: If they come one after the other, everyone agrees they are pure.
They argued only
when one person comes to ask about himself and about his friend:
One Sage compares it to 'at the same time,'
phrases.notes: This first Sage is רבי יוסי, who calls them impure. The other Sage in the next line is רבי יהודה, who calls them pure.

phrases.aramaic: וּמָר מְדַמֵּי לֵיהּ לְבָזֶה אַחַר זֶה.
phrases.english: and the other Sage compares it to 'one after the other.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Makes the argument in step 23 narrower and sets up the key idea of 'at the same time.'
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Together: everyone says impure. One after the other: everyone says pure. One person asking about both: this is the argument.

steps.title: Permitting every wife counts as 'at the same time'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא applies רבא's rule: permitting all the wives because of one small hiding place is like judging them all together, so they should be forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: And here too, since he permits all of them, it is like 'at the same time'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its challenge. Permitting every woman because of a hiding place that fits only one is like judging them all at once.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Everyone agrees that 'at the same time' leads to the strict ruling. A ruling that permits all the wives together, when only one could have hidden, is like asking about everyone at once. So the wives should not all be permitted.
steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא suggests that permitting every wife because of a hiding place that fits only one is like judging everyone 'at the same time,' which everyone agrees is strict. The next step rejects this comparison.

phrases.english: And here too,
since he permits all of them,
it counts as 'at the same time'!

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהָכָא נָמֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּשָׁרֵי לְהוּ לְכוּלְּהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Applies רבא's 'at the same time' rule from step 24 to רבי ירמיה's question.
steps.kashyaTarget: The option in step 21 that each woman is permitted with 'she is the one who hid.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ruling that permits everyone is like judging all of them together. Everyone agrees that judging together is strict, so they should not be permitted.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: According to this challenge, a hiding place that fits only one woman would not permit all the wives. Step 26 rejects the comparison.

steps.title: The two-paths case is different because there the impurity is certain
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison to the two paths. There, impurity definitely exists. Here, maybe no woman was defiled at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: How can you compare them? There, there is definitely impurity. Here, who says any woman was defiled?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the challenge from step 25 and says the two-paths case is not a fair comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the two-paths case, one path was surely impure, so one of the two people is surely impure, and judging them together forbids both. In the captured city, it is possible that no woman was defiled at all. So we are not stuck with a known problem we must place on someone, and each wife can rely on the hiding place.

keyTerms.meaning: "How can you say that?" A phrase that rejects a comparison.
"Who says?" Meaning it is not certain

steps.whatToRemember: Judging everyone together only forbids them when the problem surely happened to someone. When it is possible that nothing happened at all, each wife can rely on the hiding place.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not rejecting רבא's rule about asking together. It only says that rule does not fit here, because here the problem may never have happened.

phrases.english: How can these be compared?!
There, there is certainly impurity,
phrases.notes: "There" is the two-paths case. One of the two paths was definitely impure.

phrases.english: here, who says that she was defiled?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison that step 25 used to forbid all the wives.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects the use of the two-paths case for the hiding-place question. It does not reject the two-paths ruling itself.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: In the two-paths case the impurity is certain. In the captured city it is not certain that any woman was defiled.

steps.title: What if a woman says she neither hid nor was defiled?
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי asks about a woman married to a כהן who admits she did not hide but says she was still not defiled. The גמרא starts to suggest a principle for the answer.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי asked: if she said, "I did not hide and I was not defiled," what is the law? Do we say:
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי opens a new question about a woman who gives up the hiding-place claim but still says she was not defiled. The last words, "Do we say," set up a principle the גמרא is about to suggest.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now the woman was permitted because she could have hidden. Here she herself says she did not hide, so that reason seems to be gone. רב אשי asks whether her own word that she was not defiled is still believed.

keyTerms.meaning: Asks, raises a question the speaker is unsure about
I was defiled. Here it means violated, which forbids her to her husband the כהן.
"What is it?" What is the law?
"Do we say?" Opens a possible reason for the answer

phrases.english: Rav Ashi raises a question:
If she said: I did not hide
phrases.notes: She is a כהן's wife in the captured city where there was a hiding place.

phrases.english: and I was not defiled, what is the law?
Do we say:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the hiding place was shown to permit the wives, רב אשי asks about a woman who admits she did not use it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is a woman believed that she was not defiled when she herself admits she did not hide?
